summary: This informational document defines terminology for benchmarking devices that control traffic by classifying packets on defined criteria. The terminology applies to data plane measurements. Classification rules can use any IP header field, such as the DSCP, or payload fields such as port number.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4689 gives testers shared terms for describing how a network device handles traffic, including when it is congested. It emphasizes what leaves the device, because input measurements alone cannot show whether congestion affected forwarding.

questions: how to measure device congestion behavior
subtitle: Shared terms for measuring traffic-control devices under congestion.

tldr.problem: Existing benchmark terms often assume that a device is not congested. They do not describe enough about what leaves the device when traffic exceeds its forwarding ability.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4689 defines terms for configuration, measurements, packet sequence tracking, and traffic vectors. Its measurements observe both ingress and egress, with particular attention to egress during congestion.
tldr.outcome: The terms support descriptions of data-plane traffic-control behavior. End-to-end and service-level measurements are outside this document's scope.

sections.title: Why Measure Traffic at Both Ends
sections.content:
Earlier benchmark terms often assume that traffic is not congested and that packets receive one per-hop behavior. RFC 4689 adds terminology for measurements during congestion, when a device or system may be offered more traffic than it can forward.

Measurements are made at both the ingress and egress of the device or system under test. The RFC focuses on egress behavior during congestion; it does not cover end-to-end or service-level measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: To see how a device handles a traffic jam, a tester needs to measure what goes in and what comes out. This document focuses on the packets that leave the device during congestion.

sections.title: Classification, Congestion and Flows
sections.content:
Classification selects packets using defined rules. Rules may use IP header fields, packet payload fields such as a port number, or the ingress interface. Classification determines the per-hop behavior and traffic conditioning applied to a packet.

Forwarding congestion occurs when one or more egress interfaces are offered more packets than they forward. A flow contains packets that share an intended ingress and egress interface and some common network-layer content. Congestion management uses per-hop behaviors to avoid or reduce congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: A device first sorts packets using rules, then applies the configured treatment. A flow groups packets that enter and leave through the same device interfaces.

sections.title: Capacity, Delay and Jitter
sections.content:
Forwarding Capacity is the packet rate observed at egress when the device sends offered packets to the correct interface without dropping any. It differs from throughput, which is measured at ingress and does not account for queuing. Forwarding delay runs from the last bit of an input IP packet being offered to the last bit of its output packet being received.

Jitter is the absolute difference between the forwarding delays of two consecutive received packets in the same stream. A conforming packet is within specified rate, delay, or jitter bounds; a nonconforming packet is outside those bounds. Packet loss, rather than increased delay alone, is the black-box indicator of forwarding congestion in this methodology.
sections.plainLanguage: Forwarding capacity counts packets that successfully leave the device without loss. Delay measures how long a packet takes through it, and jitter measures how much that delay changes between packets.

sections.title: Tracking Packets and Describing Traffic
sections.content:
A test sequence number in each packet's payload lets a receiver check packet order within a stream. The RFC distinguishes packets received in sequence, out of order, and more than once. A duplicate packet has a sequence number already received; multicast copies sent once on different egress interfaces are not duplicates by this definition.

A vector groups packets that match classification criteria and associates them with benchmark metrics. An offered vector describes the attempted input rate. Expected vectors describe predicted forwarding, loss, delay, or jitter; output vectors describe what the device actually forwards or loses.
sections.plainLanguage: Test numbers let the receiver tell whether packets arrived in order, were reordered, or appeared twice. Vectors organize measurements by traffic class so expected behavior can be compared with observed results.
